subject: orthopaedics
title: Developmental dysplasia of the hip: clunks to osteotomies

steps.tx: Developmental dysplasia is more common in **girls**, first born babies, breech presentations and families with a previous case, so these infants need hip screening. **Barlow** testing feels for a hip that can be pushed out of the socket, while **Ortolani** testing lifts a dislocated hip back in with a palpable clunk. Unequal thigh folds (Galeazzi sign), limited abduction during a nappy change and a telescoping unstable hip all raise concern. Soft clicks without instability are usually benign. Examine every newborn and recheck at six weeks, and record stability findings clearly.
steps.say: Developmental dysplasia of the hip affects girls, first born babies, breech deliveries and positive family history more often, so you should screen these infants with extra care. On examination you can push an unstable hip out of joint with the Barlow manoeuvre, and you can lift a dislocated hip back into the socket with the Ortolani manoeuvre, which produces a felt clunk. Unequal thigh skin folds, limited abduction when you change the nappy, and a hip that telescopes on gentle traction all point toward instability, whereas an isolated soft click with a stable hip is usually harmless. You must examine every newborn hip and review it again at about six weeks, documenting stability findings in the notes.

steps.tx: Ultrasound uses the **Graf** method, where an alpha angle of sixty degrees marks a mature hip and the beta angle reflects the roof cartilage. Dynamic Harcke stress views test stability during movement. The **Pavlik** harness is first treatment under six months, holding hips flexed and abducted. Success needs nursing inside the **Ramsey** safe zone, with weekly checks of the femoral nerve and ultrasound position. If the harness fails, closed reduction under imaging with a spica cast follows, since prolonged malposition risks avascular injury of the femoral head.
steps.say: On ultrasound the Graf method grades maturity, with an alpha angle around sixty degrees marking a mature hip and the beta angle describing the roof cartilage, while dynamic Harcke views test whether the hip stays stable during stress. The Pavlik harness is the standard first treatment in babies under six months because it cradles both hips in flexion and abduction. You must keep the hips inside the Ramsey safe zone and review the femoral nerve and the ultrasound position every week. When the harness cannot hold the reduction, you move to closed reduction under imaging followed by a spica cast, since prolonged malposition can injure the blood supply of the femoral head.

steps.tx: The photograph shows a supine infant correctly nursed in a **Pavlik** harness, which is the image you must recognise in the exam. A **chest halter** anchors the frame while anterior flexion straps and posterior abduction straps position each leg. The green overlay marks the **Ramsey** safe zone of combined flexion and abduction where the dislocated hip stays reduced. Hips nursed inside this arc remodel the socket safely, while forced abduction outside it threatens the femoral nerve and the head blood supply.
steps.say: This photograph shows an infant lying supine in a Pavlik harness, and you should learn to name each part for the exam. The chest halter anchors the frame on the trunk, while the anterior straps hold flexion and the posterior straps hold abduction of each leg. The green shaded arc marks the Ramsey safe zone, which is the range of flexion and abduction where the hip stays reduced and the socket remodels. You must nurse every harness within this arc, because forced abduction beyond it can injure the femoral nerve and disturb blood supply to the femoral head.

steps.tx: When closed care fails, traction with an **arthrogram** confirms concentric seating, and adductors may need release before reduction. Open reduction uses a medial or anterolateral approach when seating proves impossible. Pelvic cover is rebuilt by osteotomy: the **Salter** cut rotates the socket, the **Pemberton** cut hinges the roof over the head, and the Dega cut adds posterior cover. Older children may need femoral varus derotation with shortening, and teenagers may gain a shelf augmentation. A moulded human position spica holds the hip, changed under anaesthesia, with abduction bracing during rehabilitation.
steps.say: When closed treatment fails, you should confirm under traction with an arthrogram that the femoral head seats concentrically, and you may need to release tight adductors before the hip will reduce. Open reduction through a medial or anterolateral approach becomes necessary when closed seating proves impossible. Surgeons then rebuild socket cover with a pelvic osteotomy, rotating the socket in a Salter cut, hinging the roof downward in a Pemberton cut, or adding posterior cover with a Dega cut. Older children may also need femoral varus derotation with shortening, while teenagers can gain extra cover from a shelf procedure. You hold the hip in a moulded human position spica, change the cast under anaesthesia, and continue abduction bracing through rehabilitation.

steps.tx: Neglected dysplasia presents in walkers with a **Trendelenburg** lurch and a short limb, managed with shoe raises and gait analysis. A femur left long may need shortening, and redundant capsule is tightened by capsulorrhaphy. Teenagers with preserved joints suit a Ganz periacetabular osteotomy (**PAO**) that reorients the socket. Worn hips need early total hip replacement (**THR**), staged when both sides are involved. Counsel families about recurrence, screen siblings, and keep every replaced or observed hip under lifelong follow up with arthroplasty registration.
steps.say: Children with neglected dysplasia start walking with a Trendelenburg lurch and a short limb, so you should measure leg lengths, prescribe shoe raises, and arrange gait analysis. A femur left long may need surgical shortening, and a redundant capsule is tightened with capsulorrhaphy. Teenagers whose joints are still preserved can benefit from a Ganz periacetabular osteotomy that reorients the socket over the head. Hips that are already worn need early total hip replacement, staged when both sides are affected. You should counsel families about recurrence, screen siblings, and keep every hip under lifelong follow up with arthroplasty registration.
